rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi distinguishes four answer forms: replies introduced by qul, by fa-qul, questions with no stated answer, and answers without either formula; he illustrates them with the cited questions.
rows.anchor: فالأغلب فيها أنه سبحانه وتعالى لما ذكر السؤال قال لمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم قل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit command qul functions as a seal confirming Muhammad's prophethood and honoring him as God's addressee for delivering revelation.
rows.anchor: لأن قوله تعالى قل كالتوقيع المحدد في ثبوت نبوة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the mountain question concerns eternity or necessary existence, God commands an immediate answer; each part can be destroyed and sensory evidence shows this, so the whole is not eternal or necessary.
rows.anchor: هذه المسألة من أمهات مسائل أصول الدين فلا جرم أمر الله تعالى محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The answer to the question about God's substance lacks fa because the question is not quoted there; fa is a conjunction and requires preceding speech, unlike the quoted mountain question.
rows.anchor: وحرف الفاء من الحروف العاطفة فيستدعي سبق كلام فلما لم يوجد ترك الفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God leaves the question about the Hour's exact time unanswered because knowing it has harms, showing that some questions receive no answer.
rows.anchor: فالحكمة فيه أن معرفة وقت الساعة على التعيين مشتملة على المفاسد

words: وإذا سألك عبادي عني فإني قريب
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike ordinary stories, whose retelling Muhammad is commanded to deliver, the prayer answer omits qul to show that no intermediary stands between God and the supplicant; God speaks directly.
rows.anchor: والحاصل كأنه سبحانه وتعالى قال : يا محمد إذا سئلت عن غيري فكن أنت المجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording shows that a servant may ask God and that God is near the servant.
rows.anchor: يدل على أن العبد له ( أن يسأل ) وقوله : { فإني قريب } يدل على أن الرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nearness belongs to God, not to the contingent servant: the servant is rooted in nonexistence, and God brings him into being and draws him near through grace.
rows.anchor: لم يقل فالعبد مني قريب ، بل قال أنا منه قريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses had received six demanding charges: knowledge of oneness, worship and prayer, the Hereafter, wisdom in God's acts, great signs, and a mission to the most defiant people.
rows.anchor: أحدها : معرفة التوحيد : { إننى أنا الله لا إلاه إلا أنا }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that Moses sought nearness to offset the crushing weight of these duties; he also feared human and jinn devils and sought safety through supplication.
rows.anchor: فكانت هذه التكاليف الشاقة سببا للقهر فأراد موسى عليه السلام جبر هذا القهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second explanation: on his way to Pharaoh, Moses sought to cut off creatures' hopes in him, knowing that God draws near those who call on Him.
rows.anchor: أراد الذهاب إلى فرعون وقومه فأراد أن يقطع طمع الخلق عن نفسه بالكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third, metaphysical reading treats created things as darkness and nonbeing; Moses asks for the light of knowledge in his heart, after which he sees no other existence, so he next asks that his work be made easy.
rows.anchor: الوجود كالنور والعدم كالظلمة وكل ما سوى الله تعالى فهو عدم محض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth explanation asks God to strengthen Moses' weak inner sight with the sun of divine aid, enabling him to see things as they are, like Muhammad's reported prayer.
rows.anchor: عين العين ضعيفة فأطلع يا إلهي شمس التوفيق حتى أرى كل شيء كما هو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expansion of the chest prepares the heart for divine lights, just as listening prepares for understanding; after God told Moses to listen to revelation, Moses asked for the other prerequisite.
rows.anchor: شرح الصدر مقدمة لسطوع الأنوار الإلهية في القلب والاستماع مقدمة الفهم الحاصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says li, 'for me,' so the benefit of the expanded chest accrues to Moses rather than God.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل رب اشرح صدري ليظهر أن منفعة ذلك الشرح عائدة إلى موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Razi defers comparison between the expansion of Moses' chest and Muhammad's chest to his commentary on 94:1.
rows.anchor: وأما كيفية شرح صدر رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم والمفاضلة بينه وبين شرح صدر موسى

rows.speaker: أهل السنة
rows.claim: The Sunnis explain Moses' request for ease as asking God to create ease in his affair.
rows.anchor: والمراد منه عند أهل السنة خلقها وعند المعتزلة تحريك الدواعي والبواعث

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Mu'tazilites interpret the request as God activating motives and incentives through facilitative acts of grace.
rows.anchor: عند المعتزلة تحريك الدواعي والبواعث بفعل الألطاف المسهلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although God has already done every grace that could be done, some graces may only properly be given after this request; asking makes their provision fitting.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن يكون هناك من الألطاف ما لا يحسن فعلها إلا بعد هذا السؤال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lack of a conjunction between 'created man' and 'taught him speech' makes the second phrase explain the first: being taught articulate speech defines human creation as rational speech.
rows.anchor: لأنه لو عطفه عليه لكان مغايرا له ، أما إذا ترك الحرف العاطف

rows.speaker: زهير
rows.claim: Zuhayr's verse says a man's tongue and heart each make up half of him, with only flesh and blood remaining.
rows.anchor: قال زهير : لسان الفتى نصف ونصف فؤاده

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali says that without the tongue a person is merely an unattended beast or an embodied image; without mental perception and speech, only animal capacity remains.
rows.anchor: وقال علي : ما الإنسان لولا اللسان إلا بهيمة مهملة أو صورة ممثلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A saying makes a person's two defining small parts the heart and the tongue.
rows.anchor: وقالوا : المرء بأصغريه قلبه ولسانه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying describes a person as concealed beneath his tongue.
rows.anchor: وقال صلى الله عليه وسلم : ( المرء مخبوء تحت لسانه )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the contest between Adam and the angels, Adam's superiority became manifest through his speech when he named the things.
rows.anchor: أن في مناظرة آدم مع الملائكة ما ظهرت الفضيلة إلا بالنطق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul receives unseen forms from the angelic realm through thought, then conveys them to the physical world through speech; thought is a great act of worship, and speech is its noble means of teaching others.
rows.anchor: روحه من عالم الملائكة فهو يستفيد أبدا صور المغيبات من عالم الملائكة ثم بعد تلك الاستفادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The requests form a sequence: chest expansion gives spiritual light, ease facilitates acquiring it, and the tongue then conveys that spiritual perfection to others.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى طلب النور الواقع في الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saying 'an hour of reflection is better than a year of worship' presents thought as an especially noble means of receiving spiritual knowledge.
rows.anchor: فكذلك الواسطة في الإفادة يجب أن تكون أشرف الأعضاء فقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since knowledge is the best created thing and giving is among the best acts, the tongue, which gives knowledge as the hand gives material gifts, is the noblest organ; a saying favors the giving hand.
rows.anchor: العلم أفضل المخلوقات على ما ثبت والجود والإعطاء أفضل الطاعات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The saying that the upper hand is better than the lower hand supports the analogy between giving material goods and giving knowledge by speech.
rows.anchor: اليد العليا خير من اليد السفلى

rows.speaker: النبي عليه السلام
rows.claim: A Prophetic saying praises silence as wisdom, though few practice it; another report portrays the body's organs warning the tongue to fear God.
rows.anchor: قوله عليه السلام : ( الصمت حكمة وقليل فاعله )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Speech has four classes: harmful, equally harmful and useful, predominantly useful, or wholly useful; the first must be avoided, the second is blameworthy, and safely extracting the benefits of the last two is difficult, so silence is preferable.
rows.anchor: أن الكلام على أربعة أقسام منه ما ضرره خالص أو راجح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tongue can affirm or deny any existent or imagined subject, while each other organ reaches only its own limited sensory domain; its wide reach creates room for both good and evil and makes restraint preferable.
rows.anchor: ما من موجود أو معدوم خالق أو مخلوق معلوم أو موهوم إلا واللسان يتناوله ويتعرض له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣamt is the broadest term and applies both to those able to speak and those unable; sukūt is a speaker's silence, inṣāt combines silence with listening, and iṣāgha is listening to something faint or distant.
rows.anchor: فأما الصمت فهو أعمها لأنه يستعمل فيما يقوى على النطق وفيما لا يقوى عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inṣāt requires both listening and silence; when either is absent, it is not called inṣāt, as the verse joins listening and attentive silence.
rows.anchor: والانصات سكوت مع استماع ومتى انفك أحدهما عن الآخر لا يقال له إنصات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Silence as mere absence has no virtue; speech itself is a virtue whose vice lies in how it is used, as Moses' prayer to loosen his tongue shows.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الصمت عدم ولا فضيلة فيه بل النطق في نفسه فضيلة والرذيلة في محاورته

none: Qur'anic verses are quoted without commentary in this segment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse appears to say one thing is created from another, contrary to the apparent position of theologians; if this means replacing one attribute of a substance with another, it is possible and unobjectionable.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الآية يدل على أن الشيء قد يكون مخلوقا من الشيء وظاهر قول المتكلمين يأباه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Returning to earth means returning to graves, which are earth's place for everyone who dies; those raised to heaven could also be returned to earth later.
rows.anchor: فلا شبهة في أن المراد الإعادة إلى القبور حتى تكون الأرض مكانا وظرفا لكل من مات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closest reading of bringing people forth from earth again is resurrection and the gathering of the dead.
rows.anchor: أحدها : وهو الأقرب : { ومنها نخرجكم } يوم الحشر والبعث

rows.speaker: بعض الأخبار
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation is that people are brought out as dust and clay and then revived.
rows.anchor: وثانيها : ومنها نخرجكم ترابا وطينا ثم نحييكم بعد الإخراج

rows.speaker: البراء
rows.claim: Al-Bara' reports that after a funeral the Prophet described grave punishment, the believer's and unbeliever's questioning, and the soul's return to the body and earth; God then recalls creating, returning, and raising people from earth. Razi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: عن البراء قال : ( خرجنا مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في جنازة رجل من الأنصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage enumerates earth's benefits: it is a bed for movement, has routes for travel, grows food and animal fodder, is humanity's origin, and becomes its container at death.
rows.anchor: عدد في هذه الآيات منافع الأرض وهي أنه تعالى جعلها لهم فراشا ومهادا

rows.speaker: النبي عليه السلام
rows.claim: The Prophet says people should treat the earth kindly because it has treated them kindly.
rows.anchor: ومن ثم قال عليه السلام : ( بروا بالأرض فإنها بكم برة )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reported view identifies the Day of Adornment as their festival, when they dressed up.
rows.anchor: أنه يوم عيد لهم يتزينون فيه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil identifies the Day of Adornment as Nowruz.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل يوم النيروز . وثالثها

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr identifies it as a market day for them.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير يوم سوق لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the day as Ashura.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس يوم عاشوراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb is read with yāʾ or tāʾ: it can mean Pharaoh gathers the people, or people are gathered; its pronoun may refer to Pharaoh in royal address or after addressing the crowd.
rows.anchor: وقرىء وأن يحشر الناس بالياء والتاء يريد وأن تحشر الناس يا فرعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses chose that public festival so God's word and religion would prevail and falsehood be humiliated before witnesses, spreading the remarkable event through settled and nomadic communities.
rows.anchor: وإنما أوعدهم ذلك اليوم ليكون علو كلمة الله تعالى وظهور دينه وكبت الكافر

rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi says the verse specifies both the day, the Day of Adornment, and its particular time, the forenoon.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي : إنه عين اليوم بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tawalla can mean turning away or departing; here it most likely means Pharaoh departed Moses at their agreed meeting time.
rows.anchor: والظاهر ههنا أنه بمعنى الانصراف وهو مفارقته موسى عليه السلام على الموعد

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil instead understands Pharaoh to have turned away from the truth and persisted in his rejection.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : فتولى أي أعرض وثبت على إعراضه عن الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh's plot encompasses the sorcerers and everyone who gathered for the contest, along with their equipment and the implements the sorcerers brought.
rows.anchor: دخل تحت قوله : { فجمع كيده } السحرة وسائر من يجتمع لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh came to the contest location accompanied by the sorcerers, the gathered people, and their equipment.
rows.anchor: دخل تحت أتى الموضع بالسحرة وبالقوم وبالآلات

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says there were seventy-two sorcerers, each carrying a rope and a staff; another report says four hundred or more, and Pharaoh watched from a seventy-cubit pavilion.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس : كانوا اثنين وسبعين ساحرا مع كل واحد منهم حبل وعصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative count gives four hundred sorcerers or more; Pharaoh sat watching them from a pavilion seventy cubits long.
rows.anchor: وقيل كانوا أربعمائة وقيل أكثر من ذلك ثم ضربت لفرعون قبة فجلس فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses warned them before the contest not to falsely claim that his message was untrue and sorcery, thereby licensing an attempt to oppose him.
rows.anchor: قدم قبل كل شيء الوعيد والتحذير مما قالوه وأقدموا عليه

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj allows two parses of wailakum: an implicit verb meaning 'may God impose woe on you if you lie,' or a vocative, as in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : يجوز في انتصاب ويلكم أن يكون المعنى ألزمهم الله ويلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that God will punish them with a destructive, annihilating punishment.
rows.anchor: وقوله : { فيسحتكم بعذاب } أي يعذبكم عذابا مهلكا مستأصلا

rows.speaker: حمزة وعاصم والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza, Asim, and al-Kisa'i read the yāʾ with ḍamma, using the form from isḥāt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة وعاصم والكسائي برفع الياء من الإسحات والباقون بفتحها

rows.speaker: الباقون
rows.claim: The other readers use fatḥa on the yāʾ, reading the form from saḥt.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة وعاصم والكسائي برفع الياء من الإسحات والباقون بفتحها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isḥāt is the dialect of Najd and Banu Tamim, while saḥt is the Hijazi form; both convey being destroyed.
rows.anchor: والإسحات لغة أهل نجد وبني تميم والسحت لغة أهل الحجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forging lies against God brings either annihilation in this world or severe punishment in the Hereafter, and also failure and deprivation of one's aim.
rows.anchor: من افترى على الله كذبا حصل له أمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of tanaazaʿu is that they discussed and consulted until they could agree on one course.
rows.anchor: تفاوضوا وتشاوروا ليستقروا على شيء واحد

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says they disagreed among themselves about their course.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل : اختلفوا فيما بينهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some include Pharaoh and his followers in the dispute; others say only the sorcerers argued. The wording permits either, with no clear basis for preference.
rows.anchor: والكلام محتمل وليس في الظاهر ما يدل على الترجيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view is that they kept their secret counsel from Pharaoh; Ibn Abbas says they resolved to follow Moses if he defeated them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما إن نجواهم قالوا : إن غلبنا موسى اتبعناه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says they reasoned that if Moses was a sorcerer they could defeat him, but if he came from heaven he had a different matter.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة إن كان ساحرا فسنغلبه وإن كان من السماء فله أمر

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says that after Moses warned them, they remarked that this was not the speech of a sorcerer.
rows.anchor: قال وهب لما قال : { ويلكم } الآية قالوا ما هذا بقول ساحر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says they hid their counsel from both Moses and Pharaoh; the secret was their accusation that the two men were sorcerers seeking to expel them.
rows.anchor: وهو قول السدي . الوجه الثالث

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says they concealed their plan from Moses, Aaron, Pharaoh, and the people while deciding how to display the ropes and staffs for maximum effect.
rows.anchor: فيكون أوقع في القلوب للعيوب وهو قول الضحاك

none: Qur'anic verses are quoted without commentary in this segment.

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو وعيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: Abu Amr and Isa ibn Umar read inna hadhayni, a form also attributed to Uthman, Aisha, Ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Hasan.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو وعيسى بن عمر : ( إن هذين لساحران )

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Asked about this reading and forms in 5:69 and 4:162, Aisha reportedly said the written forms were scribal errors.
rows.anchor: فقالت يا ابن أخي هذا خطأ من الكاتب

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: A report says Uthman saw a grammatical error in the codex and said the Arabs would correct it with their tongues.
rows.anchor: وروي عن عثمان أنه نظر في المصحف فقال : أرى فيه لحنا وستقيمه العرب بألسنتها

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr reportedly said he was ashamed to recite the common wording inna hadhani la-sahirani.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي عمرو أنه قال : إني لأستحي أن أقرأ

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir reads in with a light nūn and doubles the nūn in hadhan.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير : ( إن هذان ) بتخفيف إن وتشديد نون هذان

rows.speaker: حفص عن عاصم
rows.claim: Hafs, transmitting from Asim, reads with both nūns light.
rows.anchor: قرأ حفص عن عاصم إن هذان بتخفيف النونين

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud's variant places the phrase after 'they kept their counsel,' uses a fatḥa on in, jussives its nūn, and omits the lām before sahiran.
rows.anchor: قرأ عبد الله بن مسعود : { وأسروا النجوى * إن هاذان } بفتح الألف وجزم نونه

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash explains light inna with the sense of heavy inna as a dialect that raises its following noun and adds a lām to distinguish it from in meaning 'not.'
rows.anchor: عن الأخفش : { قالوا إن هاذان لساحران } خفيفة في معنى ثقيلة وهي لغة قوم

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Ka'b is reported to have read 'These two are only sorcerers,' as well as inna hadhani la-sahirani and in dhani la-sahirani; al-Khalil is also cited for one form.
rows.anchor: روى عن أبي بن كعب : ( ما هذان إلا ساحران ) وروي عنه أيضا

rows.speaker: المحققون
rows.claim: The critical scholars hold that these variant readings cannot be authenticated as Qur'an because they come through solitary reports, while Qur'anic transmission must be mutawatir.
rows.anchor: هذه القراءات لا يجوز تصحيحها لأنها منقولة بطريق الآحاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If solitary reports could add Qur'anic wording, one could no longer be certain the received text is complete; allowing such variants would open the door to addition, omission, or alteration.
rows.anchor: إذ لو جوزنا إثبات زيادة في القرآن بطريق الآحاد لما أمكننا القطع بأن هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecting the widespread reading would be worse: it is transmitted as widely as the whole Qur'an, so rejecting it would undermine tawatur and the entire text, and a solitary report cannot outweigh it.
rows.anchor: لما كان نقل هذه القراءة في الشهرة كنقل جميع القرآن فلو حكمنا ببطلانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims agree that the codex text is God's speech, which cannot contain grammatical error; this refutes the reports attributed to Uthman and Aisha.
rows.anchor: أن المسلمين أجمعوا على أن ما بين الدفتين كلام الله تعالى وكلام الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari argues that the Companions would not have delegated correction of a supposed codex error to later Arabs when they warned against innovation and urged adherence; thus the common reading must be sound.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري إن الصحابة هم الأئمة والقدوة فلو وجدوا في المصحف لحنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest grammatical account is that the common reading follows a dialect of some Arabs that leaves the dual form in the nominative shape even after inna.
rows.anchor: الوجه الأول : وهو الأقوى أن هذه لغة لبعض العرب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj attributes the dialect behind the common reading to Kinanah.
rows.anchor: والزجاج نسبها إلى كنانة وقطرب نسبها إلى بلحارث بن كعب

rows.speaker: قطرب
rows.claim: Qutrub attributes the dialect to Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, Murad, Khash'am, and some of Banu Udrah.
rows.anchor: وقطرب نسبها إلى بلحارث بن كعب ومراد وخثعم وبعض بني عذرة

rows.speaker: ابن جني
rows.claim: Ibn Jinni traces this dialect to some of Banu Rabi'a.
rows.anchor: ونسبها ابن جني إلى بعض بني ربيعة أيضا وأنشد الفراء على هذه اللغة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra cited a line of Arabic poetry as evidence for this dialect; the excerpt stops before the quoted line.
rows.anchor: وأنشد الفراء على هذه اللغة
